description:
Team T-Minus Zero 🚀 
In space, fire turns into a ghostly blue ball. Cute, until you remember there’s no fire department 400 km up. We’re building an AI dashboard that turns NASA’s mountain of combustion research into clear safety answers.
I’m Steve, 3rd-year CSE (Python, AI). 
Need data viz, UI/UX, writing & video people. Rocket science degree optional.

T-minus zero.
Zero gravity, zero excuses. Join the crew.
summary: FlameAtlas is a web dashboard that makes decades of NASA microgravity combustion research easy to search, compare and rank. NASA’s ISS combustion experiments matter for fire safety on future Moon and Mars missions, but they are hard to find and interpret. FlameAtlas organizes 20 investigations (including FLEX, BASS, SoFIE, SAME and ACME) with search, category filters and a detail page for each showing objectives, fuels, hardware, test conditions, key findings and Earth applications. A Moon Base relevance score ranks investigations against planned lunar habitat conditions (30% or more oxygen, 10.2 psi or less) and explains every score criterion by criterion. Missing data is shown as “Not reported” and never guessed, and the score is labeled a heuristic, not a NASA metric.
details:
What it does: FlameAtlas turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into an interactive dashboard for students, researchers and engineers. Users can search and filter 20 investigations, open a detail page for each (objective, fuel, hardware, oxygen and pressure conditions, key findings, Earth applications), and sort by a Moon Base relevance score.

How the score works: it combines oxygen level (50%), pressure (30%) and fire-safety category (20%), compared against planned lunar habitat conditions (30%+ oxygen, 10.2 psi or less). If data is missing for a criterion, it is skipped and the other weights are rescaled. If both oxygen and pressure are missing, the investigation shows “Not scored.” Every score has a “Why this score” panel, and it is labeled a heuristic, not a NASA metric.

Data: compiled from NASA’s “A Researcher’s Guide to ISS Combustion Science” (2015) and the challenge description. Every value that is not stated in the sources is shown as “Not reported.” Some statuses (such as ACME and SoFIE “planned”) are as of the 2015 guide and are labeled that way.

Tools: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, hosted on Vercel.

Use of SI: the code was written with AI coding assistance (Cline with DeepSeek models), and the dataset and project plan were prepared with help from an AI assistant (Claude), then checked against NASA sources. The app contains no AI-generated images or video.

Limitations and next steps: PSI links still need to be added per investigation, and a partial-gravity gap view and an AI research assistant that answers only from the dataset are planned. NASA’s database currently has no partial-gravity combustion data.
